# Exercises {#sec-m4-exercicios}

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. Extracting from OSM

Extract from OpenStreetMap all the railway stations (`railway = station`) in the state of
Paraná and count how many there are. Then mark on the map those less than 20 km from the Port
of Paranaguá.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| eval: false
res <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-54.62, -26.72, -48.02, -22.52), timeout = 180) |>
  osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "railway", value = "station") |>
  osmdata::osmdata_sf()

estacoes <- res$osm_points |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(name)) |> dplyr::select(osm_id, name)
nrow(estacoes)

porto <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(c(-48.5119, -25.5016)), crs = 4326)

proximas <- estacoes[sf::st_is_within_distance(estacoes, porto, 20000, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]
proximas$name
```
:::

## 2. Generalised cost

Using the generalised cost function from @sec-m4-roteamento, compare three transport
alternatives for the same cargo between Manaus and Santos: coastal shipping (2,800 km, 12 days),
road (3,900 km, 5 days) and a combination (2,000 km of coastal shipping + 400 km by road).
Assume the per-km costs you think reasonable and **document the assumptions**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
premissas <- data.frame(
  modo          = c("cabotagem", "rodoviario"),
  custo_ton_km  = c(0.12, 0.42),
  custo_ton_dia = c(1.50, 8.00)
)

alternativas <- data.frame(
  alternativa = c("Direct coastal shipping", "Road", "Combined", "Combined"),
  modo        = c("cabotagem", "rodoviario", "cabotagem", "rodoviario"),
  km          = c(2800, 3900, 2000, 400),
  dias        = c(12, 5, 9, 1)
)

alternativas |>
  dplyr::left_join(premissas, by = "modo") |>
  dplyr::mutate(custo = km * custo_ton_km + dias * custo_ton_dia) |>
  dplyr::summarise(custo_por_tonelada = round(sum(custo), 2), .by = alternativa) |>
  dplyr::arrange(custo_por_tonelada) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The values are illustrative: the exercise is about the **structure** of the calculation and about recording
the assumptions in a way that someone else can challenge them. That is what distinguishes an analysis
from an opinion.
:::

## 3. Accessibility and income

With the `aopdata` data for Fortaleza, compute the ratio between the average access of the highest
income stratum and that of the lowest, for 30 and for 60 minutes. Does inequality increase or decrease
with the time limit?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
aop <- readRDS("dados/brutos/aop_fortaleza.rds")
col_renda <- dplyr::intersect(c("R002", "R003"), names(aop))[1]

razao <- function(col) {
  d <- aop |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
    dplyr::filter(P001 > 0, !is.na(.data[[col]]), !is.na(.data[[col_renda]])) |>
    dplyr::summarise(acesso = weighted.mean(as.numeric(.data[[col]]), P001),
                     .by = dplyr::all_of(col_renda)) |>
    dplyr::arrange(.data[[col_renda]])

  # highest stratum divided by the lowest (not the largest access by the smallest)
  d$acesso[nrow(d)] / d$acesso[1]
}

c(`30 min` = razao("CMATT30"), `60 min` = razao("CMATT60")) |> round(2)
```

The ratio usually falls as the time limit grows: with more time available, even outlying
places reach the job centres. It is an important argument, and often misused,
because "reachable in 90 minutes" is not adequate accessibility.
:::
